title: Deriving the angle-bisector identity m·b = n·c from Mathlib's Euclidean-geometry API

problemStatement.formal: \text{In an inner-product affine space } P,\ \text{given } A,B,C,D \in P\ \text{with } \mathrm{Sbtw}_{\mathbb{R}}(B,D,C)\ \text{and } \angle BAD = \angle DAC,\ \text{derive } |BD|\cdot|AC| = |DC|\cdot|AB|.
problemStatement.plain: The parent file LawOfCosinesOQ04OQ02.lean takes 'm·b = n·c' (the algebraic form of the angle-bisector theorem) as an injected hypothesis. OQ-04-OQ-02-OQ-01 asks whether this hypothesis can be derived from the actual geometric premise — namely, that AD bisects ∠BAC and D ∈ segment(B,C) — using Mathlib's EuclideanGeometry.angle and dist API.
whyMatters: Geometric grounding — bridges the algebraic-parametric idiom of the gallery's triangle-geometry proofs (Stewart, Ceva, LawOfCosines OQ-04) to Mathlib's affine-Euclidean API on actual points.
Reusable template — the same Sbtw + angle equality ⇒ side-length ratio pattern governs cevian, median, and altitude-foot identities across multiple gallery entries.

Mathlib contribution candidate — Mathlib's Geometry/Euclidean/Triangle.lean has law of cosines and pons asinorum but no angle-bisector theorem; OQ-04-OQ-02-OQ-01 produces the prototype Mathlib.Geometry.Euclidean.AngleBisector module.
Decouples proof architecture — distinguishes the two gallery idioms (real-parameter algebra vs. P-point affine) and demonstrates a clean bridge.

insights: The Sbtw ℝ B D C hypothesis provides exactly the barycentric parameter s ∈ Ioo 0 1 needed; combined with the inner-product expansion of cos(∠BAD) and cos(∠DAC), the bisector hypothesis collapses to a single algebraic equation s(b+c) = c.

The factorization ((1-s)·c - s·b)·(b·c - ⟪u,v⟫) = 0 cleanly separates the geometric content (first factor) from the degeneracy carve-out (second factor); non-collinearity (the standard Mathlib non-degeneracy predicate) discharges the second factor.

Path B (double law-of-cosines at vertex A) under-determines the conclusion: one cosine-equality equation in five real unknowns is insufficient without additional constraints. The classical bisector theorem really needs either the inner-product factorization (Path A) or the parallel-line / similarity construction (Path C).
Mathlib lacks a packaged angle-bisector theorem in either vector or affine form, so this OQ produces a natural Mathlib-contribution candidate (Mathlib.Geometry.Euclidean.AngleBisector).

The gallery's algebraic-parametric idiom (real parameters a, b, c, t, m, n, u with linear_combination witnesses) and Mathlib's affine-Euclidean idiom (P-points with dist/angle/Sbtw) are bridge-able cleanly when the algebraic identity factors over a known degenerate-case witness — as it does here.

S2 ACT scaffolding strategy: ship namespace/imports/variable-block + theorem statements first (low bearer risk), then discharge sorries lemma-by-lemma in S3 against docker-build feedback. Total Path A budget ~250-350 LOC across 4 helper lemmas + main theorem + chained S4 statement.
mathlibGaps: Mathlib.Geometry.Euclidean.Triangle has the law of cosines and pons asinorum but no angle-bisector theorem.
Mathlib has no median-length theorem, no Stewart's theorem in affine form, and no Ceva / Menelaus theorems on actual triangle points.
Mathlib has the inner-product Cauchy-Schwarz inequality but no convenient packaged form of strict Cauchy-Schwarz under non-collinearity — needs lookup or local proof.
Mathlib's law of sines exists only via the circumscribed-circle formulation in Geometry.Euclidean.Angle.Sphere (requiring [Module.Oriented ℝ V (Fin 2)]); a triangle-form law of sines is not packaged.
